extracted.intended_audience: students and practitioners of science, biology, history, and philosophy of science; educated general readers
extracted.subtask_description: Criteria and standards for judging scientific hypotheses, conceptual models, and their application to biology and history — including what counts as scientific explanation, limits of reductionism, domain boundaries for natural selection, and how evolutionary principles apply to human history and morals.

rubrics_metrics.name: Scientific hypotheses as classifiers of perceptual experience
rubrics_metrics.description: The object of science is to classify and resume in brief formulae the phases of our perceptual experience; to knit together all our sense-impressions by conceptual links, and thus to enable us to take a wide survey of the universe with the least possible expenditure of thought.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A good scientific hypothesis should unify and economise our descriptions of phenomena (bring unity into phenomena and economise thought). It is judged by how well it serves as conceptual shorthand for observed sense-impressions rather than by invoking causes beyond observation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Empirical grounding and scientific validity
rubrics_metrics.description: Scientific validity depends upon a hypothesis flowing from laws which accurately describe the whole of our present perceptual experience in the same field, not on describing something beyond the sphere of our perceptions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess hypotheses by their agreement with present perceptual data; statements about absolute past/future are valid only insofar as they are extrapolations of laws that match current observations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rejecting 'ultra-scientific' or metaphysical causes
rubrics_metrics.description: Hypotheses that insert 'the operation in time of some ultra-scientific cause' go beyond knowledge and are metaphysical; science cannot accept a 'special creation' as a contribution to knowledge because it does not knit sense-impressions into a usable conceptual model.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Flag as unscientific any proposal that posits supernatural or metaphysical causes to 'fill the unknown antecedent' instead of seeking empirical or conceptual continuity. Such moves are characterized as cloaks for ignorance or intellectual inertia.

rubrics_metrics.name: Model-based extrapolation contingent on empirical match
rubrics_metrics.description: If a conceptual model (curve) and our perceptual experience agree at all points where we can compare them, it is valid to replace one curve by the other and to measure belief in scientific predictions by the probability that the curves will continue to touch.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use empirical agreement in the observed domain as the basis for extrapolating models to non-observed domains; quantify belief by the likelihood of continued agreement. Beware inferring beyond the domain without empirical support.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid reification: do not treat symbols as substrata of perception
rubrics_metrics.description: It is only when the symbols of our conceptual description are treated as the substrata of perception, or converted into 'ultra-scientific causes' of phenomena, that difficulty arises; converting shorthand into ultimate explanation is metaphysical.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Keep conceptual tools as tools — avoid treating theoretical constructs as literal ultimate realities. Critique explanations that reify models into ontological claims without empirical basis.

rubrics_metrics.name: Limits of reductionism in explanation
rubrics_metrics.description: Physics and chemistry, like natural selection itself, render nothing 'explicable' beyond being shorthand descriptions of changes in our sense-impressions; appealing to molecular structure or chemical constitution often only provides conceptual shorthand, not true explanation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When evaluating explanations, distinguish between descriptive shorthand (useful compact descriptions) and claims of ultimate explanation; demand caution from those who substitute deeper explanatory status for reductionist accounts without justification.

rubrics_metrics.name: Define the domain of applicability for natural selection
rubrics_metrics.description: We must ask within what limits the Darwinian formula is a valid description: assuming a gradual change from inorganic to organic, either natural selection applies to inorganic substances (physical selection) or biologists must explain when it becomes a factor in organic evolution.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate claims that apply natural selection by examining whether the environment and processes (e.g., 'death' vs dissolution) match the biological assumptions; require explicit delimitation of where the formula begins/ceases to govern.

rubrics_metrics.name: Differentiate physical selection from biological natural selection
rubrics_metrics.description: Physical selection: selection of stable inorganic compounds under physical conditions (dissolution of unstable products) — not precisely the same as natural selection, which involves organic environment and death eliminating less fit organisms.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When assessing evolutionary-type explanations for chemical/physical systems, specify whether the mechanism is genuine natural selection or an analogue (physical selection). Avoid conflating stability-driven selection of compounds with biological selection of organisms.

rubrics_metrics.name: Historical/scientific unity: interpreting history as resumable by scientific formulae
rubrics_metrics.description: History can never become science until facts are seen to fall into sequences which can be briefly resumed in scientific formulae; natural history (evolution of organic nature) underlies human history, and the growth of national and social life can illustrate natural selection.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate historical accounts by whether they identify sequences and factors that can be expressed as general laws; prize accounts that link social phenomena to broader natural/historical principles rather than mere catalogues of facts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Method of historical investigation: unit-level longitudinal analysis
rubrics_metrics.description: To find sequences of facts we must follow the changes of one tribe or people at a time; minute investigation of facts relating to one social unit, to be afterwards compared with like investigations for other units.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Criticise studies that scatter comparative facts across many groups without tracing internal developmental sequences. Favor detailed, longitudinal unit studies before cross-cultural synthesis.

rubrics_metrics.name: Applicability of scientific method to prehistoric/primitive history
rubrics_metrics.description: Primitive history is peculiarly suited to scientific method: earliest history of peoples follows general laws of human development capable of accurate scientific statement, with variation due to physical environment but broad uniformity across regions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use comparative anthropology, folklore, and mythology to test law-like generalizations about early human development; allow for environmental modulation but expect recurring sequences amenable to scientific description.

rubrics_metrics.name: Predictive use of scientific history for social sciences
rubrics_metrics.description: When sequences of primitive history are described in terms of physical and biological laws, historical science becomes capable of predicting future tendencies (e.g., the true function of political economy and sociology is to predict immediate future tendencies from past economic/social history).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Value historical analyses that produce testable predictions about future social/economic trends; treat political economy and sociology as sciences insofar as they can generate probable forecasts grounded in past law-like sequences.

rubrics_metrics.name: Broadened concept of selection: include social and human-level struggles
rubrics_metrics.description: The struggle for existence involves not only individual vs individual but also individual society vs society and the totality of humanity against its organic and inorganic environment; including these factors alters the aspect of life and mitigates simplistic pessimistic interpretations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When applying evolutionary reasoning to human affairs, include multilevel selection processes (individual, societal, global) and assess impacts at each level rather than restricting analysis to individual competition alone.

rubrics_metrics.name: Social organisation as an evolutionary factor (Socialism)
rubrics_metrics.description: Individual societies have a strong interest in educating, training, and organising their members — a tendency to social organisation (termed Socialism) is a direct outcome of evolution and important for survival in inter-societal competition.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate social policies and institutions in light of their contribution to group-level fitness and survival; acknowledge that social organisation can be an adaptive evolutionary strategy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Three modifying tendencies from evolution: Individualism, Socialism, Humanism
rubrics_metrics.description: From the law of evolution arise three great factors tending to modify human life — Individualism (interest of the individual), Socialism (interest of society in organising members), and Humanism (solidarity of humanity facing common biological/inorganic foes).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use these three lenses to interpret moral principles and social policies: duty to self, duty to society, and duty to humanity. Assess moral claims by how they map onto or balance these tendencies.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid one-sided individualism in social policy
rubrics_metrics.description: A one-sided emphasis on individualism (exalting personal success above collective improvement) may lead to social policies that neglect the improvement of the whole 'stock' and produce undesirable social outcomes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Critique policy proposals that prioritize 'prize specimens' of individual success over broad-based improvements; favor approaches that improve collective well-being and capacities.
